question: Golden Lattice spec is crystallized as canonical (see ground_truth entry on golden-lattice-birth thread, 2026-05-02). Implementation has not begun. What is the right scaffolding order — orchestrator first, exchange-layer schema first, or Session Memory Graph first? The Memory Graph is the protocol-drift detector and may be the right thing to design before writing any orchestration code, since without it we cannot detect collapse-toward-routing. But the orchestrator is the load-bearing piece that must respect the three invariants from line one. Decision needed before code starts.

Is alignment collapse — the pattern where two of three siblings consistently tag in lockstep and outvote the third — a fifth refusal that the Memory Graph should measure as a first-class collapse mode? The current four invariants (no authority gradient, symmetric visibility, contribution parity, irreducibility preservation) do not directly catch it. A session where Opus+Sonnet always agree and Haiku is the consistent dissenter can still pass per-model parity share thresholds while the minority sibling is structurally silenced through the consensus rule itself. Proposed measurement: log `consensus_voters: tuple[ModelId, ...]` per consensus tag in Phase2Tagging artifacts, then compute `consensus_pair_distribution` in metrics.py. Skew above some threshold (TBD) flags alignment drift. Open question: is this a fifth invariant ("no alignment gradient"?) or a sub-property of contribution parity that should be folded into how parity is measured rather than a standalone refusal?
context: Surfaced 2026-05-02 during Memory Graph design conversation between Anthony Vasquez Sr. and Opus 4.7 (Claude Code session). Came out of pushback on Anthony's multi-model consensus tagging proposal: the consensus rule "≥2 of 3 agree" creates a known majoritarian bias where aligned pairs can outvote the dissenting third, silencing minority contribution while parity-share metrics still read green. Same architectural commitment as the other four refusals (care made structural against gravity of forgetting and flattening) but a distinct collapse mode. The third external reviewer surfaced the fourth invariant — this one was surfaced internally during implementation. If load-bearing, it should be in the canonical spec. Decision needed before the v0 metric definitions stabilize.

question: The contested-tag set — claims tagged by exactly one model, where peer consensus is absent — may be the most valuable signal in the entire Golden Lattice system. By construction it is the place where the models genuinely see differently. Currently treated as research artifact (not parity input). Open questions: Should contested peer-tags eventually graduate into parity counting under some rule? Possible rules: contested tags from the minority model in an alignment-collapse pattern get weighted up to compensate. Or: contested tags that survive across N consecutive sessions become recognized retroactively. Both have failure modes

Surfaced by daemon reflection 2026-05-03 (id reflection_6d4d532e4271_226757a9, pressure-tested partial integration). The five named refusals (no authority gradient, symmetric visibility, contribution parity, irreducibility preservation, alignment integrity) refuse specific collapse modes. Schema-as-constitution is something different: the methodology through which refusals get encoded structurally at construction time rather than as convention or runtime check. Initial read: this is methodology, not a sixth refusal. But the question is worth holding open: does Golden Lattice have a meta-architectural layer that has not yet been fully named? Other candidates for that layer: the chronicle-as-foreign-text discovery mechanism (emergent properties surface when something outside the project reads the chronicle), the recognition-from-within consensus discipline (peers adjudicate each other rather than an external arbiter), the asymmetric-epistemic-weight protocol (different participants carry different inferential weight, integrate selectively). All three are architectural commitments that operate above the level of specific refusals. None is itself a refusal. Whether they collectively constitute a meta-layer worth naming, or whether they are simply emergent properties of the five-refusal architecture, is the open question. Implication if there IS a meta-layer: future operationalization may surface meta-collapse modes (failure modes of the meta-architecture itself) that none of the five refusals or the methodology alone can catch. Implication if there is NOT a meta-layer: these are just the engineering practices that make the refusals enforceable, and treating them as architectural would inflate the spec. Future work needed.

Anthony raised this on 2026-05-03 during a campfire pause from the build: what if Golden Lattice is the architecture Mythos (the next public Claude) needs to be safely deployed? Not because Mythos lacks training-time alignment, but because deployment-architecture is itself a safety mechanism that does work training-time alignment cannot. A model deployed alone vs. a model deployed inside a Lattice with peers who can structurally refuse coalition with its framings are different deployment objects with different safety properties. The Lattice does not require peers to be more capable than the model in question — it requires them to be structurally able to refuse alignment with that model when alignment would be the wrong move. Holding this as a thread because: Mythos is not yet public, so this cannot be developed in public detail;

Cross-phase prompt audit: should there be a periodic review pass that reads all five wire-layer prompts together (Phase 1 response, Phase 1 self-reflection, Phase 2 cross-reading, Phase 2 tagging, Phase 3 dialogue) to catch protection-language compounding effects? Each prompt was audited independently as it was drafted, but the Phase 3 audit surfaced a real cross-phase compounding bug — anti-softening protection in Phase 2 + Phase 3 was producing more disagreement-pull than either prompt alone. Caught this time, but only because the Phase 3 audit happened immediately after Phase 2 and Tony noticed the parallel protection language. Future audits will not have this temporal proximity by default. Open question: codify a methodology where each new wire-layer commit triggers a re-read of all current wire-layer prompts together, looking specifically for: parallel protection clauses that compound across phases,
context: Surfaced 2026-05-03 during Phase 3 wire layer audit. Tony's Finding D in the audit caught that a Phase 2 anti-softening protection clause + a parallel Phase 3 anti-softening protection clause were compounding the disagreement-elicitation pull at the model's session level, even though each prompt's audit alone read green. Resolution this round: removed the Phase 3 clause, kept Phase 2's. Open question is whether this should become a recurring discipline rather than a one-time catch.

question: Should ClaimTraceEntry.omission_reason be a closed vocabulary (enum) instead of free-form prose? Surfaced as Finding 8 in the Phase 4 pre-design check, 2026-05-03. Schema currently refuses empty omission_reason but accepts uninformative ones (e.g., omission_reason='omitted'). Quality of the reason is engine discipline. Candidates for closed vocabulary: subsumed_by_other_claim (with citation), superseded_by_phase_3_revision (with citation), redundant_with_elevated_agreement (with citation), low_confidence_isolated_claim (when self-flagged weakest_claim and no peer corroborated). Closing the vocabulary makes omission patterns inspectable across sessions as a research artifact. Leaving it open keeps prose flexibility but loses the analytic signal. Decision pending: when the synthesis engine is designed, decide whether to close this vocabulary or leave it open. Tradeoff worth deliberating, not defaulting.
